[Lemma, Isaiah 7:17:] But the Lord will bring upon you, and upon your people, and upon the house of your father days which have not yet come, from the day on which Ephraim took away from Judah: the king of the Assyrians. To Ahaz, very much troubled at the agreement of the two kings, Rezin and Pekah, the God of all was promising the help; and since he wished to establish him further into faith, he ordered him to ask a sign, into depth or into height. But Ahaz refusing, and saying most perversely: I will not ask, nor will I test the Lord (for he was seeking rather the trickeries from the false seers), God in a certain manner came forward of his own accord, and himself was giving a sign to the house of David. For he was saying: Behold the virgin will have in womb, and will bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel. And since the word about these things was very well completed, he moves again the foretelling of the things to be onto the very person of Ahaz. For it was needed, it was needed, that the proclamation beforehand of the salvation through Christ come to be toward those from the house of David, that is, those from the tribe of Judah, from which Christ himself also rose according to the flesh; but of the terrible and dreaded things that will happen in times he makes the proclamation beforehand to those who chose to disobey, so that they might know that it is truly bitter, and not without penalty, for those who dishonour the divine glory to provide a contest to the Lord, and to choose to worship beside him others, the gods that are not. That then in times both Jerusalem itself and the whole country of the Jews were going to fall into the last miseries, and to come under the hand of the enemies, he announces beforehand finely. And the arrangement of the words being more unclear, as I may be able, and before the other things, I will try to make it plain. God will bring, he says, upon you, and upon your people, and upon the house of your father, days which have not yet come, from the day on which Ephraim took away from Judah. And such is the sense of the lines: in times of the reign of Rehoboam son of Solomon, Ephraim took away, that is, tore himself away, that is, again the ten tribes, from the tribe of Judah. For they were separated, and the ten tribes from the tribe of Judah dwelt in Samaria, and the tribe of Judah and the half of tribe of Manasseh remained in Jerusalem. pass_b_english: “But the Lord will bring upon you, and upon your people, and upon the house of your father, days that have not yet come, from the day that Ephraim took away from Judah: the king of the Assyrians” (Isaiah 7:17).

Ahaz was greatly alarmed at the alliance of the two kings, Rezin and Pekah, and the God of all promised him help. Since he wished to establish him further in faith, he told him to ask for a sign, “in the depth or in the height” (Isaiah 7:11). But Ahaz refused, and said most perversely, “I will not ask, nor will I put the Lord to the test” (Isaiah 7:12), for he was looking instead for the trickery of false prophets. So God in a way came forward of his own accord and himself gave a sign to the house of David. For he said: “Behold, the virgin will be with child and will bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Isaiah 7:14).

When the word about these things had been fully completed, he turns the prediction of what was to come back to the person of Ahaz himself. For it was necessary, truly necessary, that the announcement of the salvation through Christ be made to those of the house of David, that is, to those of the tribe of Judah, from which Christ himself arose according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14). But the announcement of the terrible and dreaded things that would happen in due time he makes to those who had chosen to disobey, so that they might know that it is truly bitter, and not without cost, for those who dishonor the divine glory to weary the Lord (Isaiah 7:13), and to choose to worship, in place of him, others who are not gods.

So he subtly signals in advance that in time Jerusalem itself, and the whole land of the Jews, would fall into the worst miseries and come under the hand of their enemies. Since the arrangement of the words is rather obscure, I will try, as far as I am able, to make it clear before anything else.

“God will bring,” he says, “upon you, and upon your people, and upon the house of your father, days that have not yet come, from the day that Ephraim took away from Judah.” The sense of the lines is this: in the times of the reign of Rehoboam son of Solomon, Ephraim “took away,” that is, tore itself away (Ephraim meaning, again, the ten tribes) from the tribe of Judah. For they were separated: the ten tribes, parted from the tribe of Judah, settled in Samaria, while the tribe of Judah and the half-tribe of Manasseh remained in Jerusalem.
